title: Missing Number Sums for Grade 2: Early Algebra Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Missing Number Sums Grade 2 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach missing number sums to Grade 2 the easy way: balance the equals sign, use inverse operations, and crack pattern rules. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: A blank in a sum is a child’s first taste of algebra. Here is how I teach Grade 2 to solve 7 + _ = 12 by balancing both sides and working backwards, plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 7 + _ = 12 on a slate and watch a seven-year-old’s face. Most will stare at the plus sign, add 7 and 12, and cheerfully write 19 in the blank. That is not a silly mistake — it is the exact moment a child meets algebra for the first time, and misses. Missing number sums for Grade 2 are the quiet start of algebraic thinking: the blank is an unknown, and the child’s job is to work out what it must be, not just crunch the numbers in front of them.

I have taught this to plenty of Grade 2 children in Tier-2 city classrooms, and the breakthrough always comes from one idea, not a trick. Once they see what the equals sign actually promises, the blanks stop being scary.

The equals sign is a balance, not a ‘the answer is’ button

Here is the root of the 19 mistake. To most young children, = means ‘now write the total’, because that is all they have ever seen: 7 + 5 = 12, answer on the right. So when the blank is on the right, they keep adding.

The fix is to redefine the symbol out loud, every day, for a week: the equals sign means both sides weigh the same. I use an old pan balance, or just two hands. Put 7 and something on the left; put 12 on the right. The two pans must sit level. So the blank is asking: what do I add to 7 to make the left pan match the 12 on the right? That reframing — from ‘calculate’ to ‘balance’ — is the whole game.

Try the true-or-false test

Before any blanks, I write full sentences and ask if they are true: is 6 + 4 = 10 true? Is 6 + 4 = 11 true? Is 10 = 6 + 4 true? That last one throws them, because the total is on the left. Sitting with 10 = 6 + 4 for a few minutes does more for algebra than a page of ordinary sums.

Missing number sums for Grade 2: the two ways to solve them

Once a child accepts the balance idea, there are two honest routes to the answer. I teach both, because different blanks suit different methods.

1. Count up or think of the bond

For 7 + _ = 12, ask ‘how many more from 7 to reach 12?’ Count on: eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve — that is 5 hops. Children who already know their number bonds will just know 7 and 5 make 12. Bonds do a lot of the heavy lifting here.

2. Use the inverse operation

This is the powerful one. Every addition sentence hides a subtraction. 7 + _ = 12 can be turned around into 12 − 7 = _, and the blank falls out: 5. Subtraction is the inverse of addition — it undoes it. For a subtraction blank like _ − 4 = 5, you add back: 5 + 4 = 9. The rule I give them is short: to find a missing start, do the opposite operation.

SentenceWhere is the blank?Turn it aroundAnswer
7 + _ = 12Second number12 − 75
_ + 6 = 15First number15 − 69
_ − 4 = 5Start number5 + 49
13 − _ = 8Amount taken13 − 85

That last row, 13 − _ = 8, is the sneaky one. The inverse is not ‘add’ here — you find the gap between 13 and 8. Do not gloss over it; the trickiest blanks are the ones that make a child stop and reason.

Function machines: what is the rule?

The other half of early algebra is patterns that grow by a hidden rule. Draw a little box — the ‘machine’ — that eats a number and spits out another. Feed it 2, out comes 5. Feed it 3, out comes 6. Feed it 10, out comes 13. What is the machine doing?

  • Line up the pairs: 2 → 5, 3 → 6, 10 → 13.
  • Ask what happens to every input, not just one.
  • Test your guess on a pair you have not used yet.

The rule is ‘add 3’. The magic is that the child works out a rule that holds for all numbers, even ones the machine has not seen. That is genuinely algebra — a rule about the general, not a single answer. Growing patterns work the same way: 2, 4, 6, 8, _ is a machine adding 2 each step.

A common trap to head off early

Watch for the child who gets the right answer for the wrong reason. A student once solved _ + 3 = 8 by writing 11, then ‘checked’ it by adding 11 and 3 and shrugging. The number was there on the page, so it felt done. Always ask them to read the finished sentence back: ‘eleven plus three equals eight — is that balanced?’ Reading it aloud catches nonsense that silent working hides. This one habit is worth more than a dozen corrected worksheets.

A simple weekly plan

Ten minutes a day, and mix it up so the child has to choose a method rather than repeat one:

  • Two days on the balance idea and true-or-false sentences.
  • Two days on missing number sums using the inverse operation.
  • One day on function machines and ‘what is the rule’.
  • Weekend: a mixed page on paper, no hints, so they decide for themselves.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly this — balancing sentences, finding the missing number with inverse operations, and spotting the rule of a pattern. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded missing-number and pattern questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Missing Number Sums Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on balancing sentences, finding the missing number, and spotting the rule. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 early algebra: missing numbers, balance and patterns

questions.q: What number goes in the blank? 7 + _ = 12
questions.explanation: The two sides must balance. Count up from 7 to 12, or do the inverse: 12 − 7 = 5.
To find the start, do the opposite of subtracting: add it back. 5 + 4 = 9.
The equals sign means both sides weigh the same. 10 really does equal 6 + 4, even with the total on the left.
Turn it around using the inverse: 15 − 6 = 9.

questions.q: A machine turns 2 into 5, 3 into 6, and 10 into 13. What is its rule?
questions.explanation: Every input goes up by 3: 2→5, 3→6, 10→13. The rule is add 3.
Find the gap between 13 and 8: 13 − 8 = 5. Here the inverse is a subtraction, not an addition.

questions.q: What comes next in the pattern? 2, 4, 6, 8, _
questions.explanation: The rule is add 2 each step, so after 8 comes 10.

questions.q: If 5 + 4 = 9 is true, which sentence is also true?
questions.explanation: Subtraction undoes addition. Since 5 + 4 = 9, taking 4 back gives 9 − 4 = 5.

faq.q: Is algebra really taught in Grade 2?
faq.a: Not with letters like x, but yes in spirit. Missing number sums such as 7 + _ = 12, balancing both sides of the equals sign, and finding the rule of a pattern are all early algebraic thinking, and they build directly toward formal algebra later.

faq.q: Why does my child add both numbers when the blank is on the right?
faq.a: Because they read the equals sign as ‘write the answer’. Re-teach it as a balance — both sides must weigh the same — using a pan balance or true-or-false sentences like ‘10 = 6 + 4’. That single shift usually fixes it.

faq.q: What is the inverse operation and why does it help?
faq.a: Subtraction undoes addition, and addition undoes subtraction. So 7 + _ = 12 becomes 12 − 7 = 5. Turning a missing-number sum around into its inverse is the most reliable method for a Grade 2 child.

A little box that takes a number in and gives a number out by a hidden rule — feed it 2 and get 5, feed it 3 and get 6. The child works out the rule (add 3) that works for every number, which is genuine algebraic reasoning.
